patient.chief_complaint: Progressive gait and cognitive decline labeled as PSP — second opinion requested because patient has not fallen from postural instability alone and tap trial was not offered
patient.history_present_illness: A 74-year-old retired mechanic was referred by his family for a second opinion. He was given a working diagnosis of progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) by a community neurologist 18 months ago, based on his gait deterioration, cognitive decline, and mildly reduced upward gaze. Since that diagnosis, no LP or tap trial has been offered, and he has continued to deteriorate. His son, who has done research on PSP and NPH, is requesting a formal workup including LP and possibly tap trial. The patient's wife notes his walking difficulties began approximately 2.5 years ago — she describes a shuffling wide-based gait with freezing at doorways, not the classic backward falls of PSP. He has had four falls — all forward, one to the side, none from pure backward postural instability. Urinary urgency and incontinence began approximately 18 months ago. His cognitive decline over the same period includes worsening forgetfulness and executive dysfunction. The community neurologist diagnosed PSP based on: mildly slow vertical saccades (though not absent), prominent falls, and gait disorder. A head MRI was reported as showing 'possible midbrain atrophy.' However, the family notes that re-review of the MRI at the academic center shows Evans index 0.36 — not mentioned in the community read. The key diagnostic challenge is distinguishing NPH from PSP, or determining whether NPH is superimposed on a PSP-spectrum disorder.

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented x3. MoCA 22/30. Mild delayed recall (2/5), executive dysfunction. Mildly reduced facial expression. No aphasia.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: PERRL. Vertical gaze: mild slowing of upward saccades — velocity reduced. Downward saccades normal velocity. NO complete vertical gaze palsy. Horizontal gaze normal. Smooth pursuit mildly saccadic. No square-wave jerks.
neurological_exam.motor: Mild symmetric axial rigidity (neck, trunk). No resting tremor. No appendicular rigidity. No cogwheel rigidity.
neurological_exam.gait: Wide-based, magnetic shuffling gait. Freezing prominent. Steps very short. TUG 34 seconds. Falls: forward and sideways — NOT predominantly backward from postural instability. Cannot tandem walk. Pull test — 2 steps backward (not extreme retropulsion).
neurological_exam.additional: Mild axial rigidity. No upper motor neuron signs. Bilateral grasp reflexes. No nuchal rigidity. Mild hypomimia.

signal_characteristics.description: Evans index 0.36 — missed on prior community read
Tight high-convexity sulci with enlarged Sylvian fissures

mri.impression: 1. Ventriculomegaly with Evans index 0.36. 2. Disproportionate sulcal effacement at high convexity with enlarged Sylvian fissures (DESH pattern). 3. Callosal angle 80 degrees. 4. Prominent aqueductal T2 flow void. 5. Midbrain-pons area ratio (MPAR) 0.55. 6. Mild periventricular FLAIR signal. No hummingbird sign. No morning glory sign. Clinical correlation recommended.

specialized_test.test_type: High-volume tap trial (40 mL) — FIRST tap trial in 2.5 years of symptoms
specialized_test.impression: Positive tap trial. TUG improved 32% at 24 hours (34 sec to 23 sec); 10-meter walk improved 35% (26 sec to 17 sec); MoCA improved 3 points (22 to 25). Decreased urgency; no incontinence in 24 hours. Clinical correlation recommended.

findings.finding: Upward saccades: velocity mildly reduced (60% of normal) but NOT absent. Downward saccades: normal velocity and accuracy. No square-wave jerks. Convergence normal. No oculomotor palsy.
Pattern: mild slowing of upward voluntary saccades. Does NOT meet MDS PSP diagnostic criteria (requires vertical supranuclear gaze palsy affecting downward saccades or complete vertical gaze palsy).

output.impression: Mild slowing of upward voluntary saccades (approximately 60% of normal velocity); downward saccades normal velocity and accuracy. No square-wave jerks. Convergence normal. No oculomotor palsy. Published MDS PSP diagnostic criteria specify vertical supranuclear gaze palsy affecting downward saccades or complete vertical gaze palsy; this examination documents mild upward slowing only. Clinical correlation recommended.

findings.result: Normal bilateral striatal dopamine transporter uptake. No putaminal or caudate loss. Normal symmetric pattern.

output.impression: Normal striatal dopamine transporter uptake. Bilateral symmetric uptake in caudate and putamen without reduction. No evidence of presynaptic dopaminergic deficit. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.modality: Formal MRI midbrain volumetry and MPAR calculation
output.impression: 1. Midbrain-pons area ratio (MPAR) 0.55 on formal T1-weighted volumetric imaging. 2. No hummingbird sign. 3. No morning glory sign. Published PSP threshold for MPAR is <0.52. No additional midbrain volume loss by formal segmentation. Clinical correlation recommended.
Negative — sparse-to-no amyloid neuritic plaque density. CL score 11, below the threshold of 24. Clinical correlation recommended.

results.title: NPH misdiagnosed as PSP — case series and distinguishing features
results.key_finding: NPH may be misdiagnosed as PSP due to overlapping gait features; key distinguishing features: (1) NPH: wide-based magnetic, forward falls, Evans index >0.3; (2) PSP: narrow-based, predominant backward falls, complete downward gaze palsy, MPAR <0.52; tap trial is diagnostic

results.title: Tap trial in suspected PSP — identifying NPH superimposition
results.key_finding: Tap trial should be performed in all patients with ventriculomegaly regardless of PSP concern; positive tap trial identifies NPH component and is a treatable finding

output.summary: PSP and NPH share overlapping gait features. Key published distinguishing features include: (1) Fall direction: NPH typically forward/sideways; PSP characteristically backward; (2) Gait morphology: NPH wide-based magnetic; PSP narrow-based with upright posture; (3) Oculomotor criteria: PSP requires downward or complete vertical gaze palsy; (4) MPAR: PSP typically <0.52 on formal measurement; (5) DaTscan: presynaptic dopaminergic deficits may be seen in PSP. Tap trial should be offered in any patient with ventriculomegaly regardless of working movement disorder diagnosis.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH) — prior PSP label not supported

differential.diagnosis: Vascular cognitive impairment / subcortical ischaemic vascular disease
differential.key_features: Small-vessel disease can produce gait apraxia and executive slowing, but ventriculomegaly out of proportion to white-matter burden and a positive tap test favour NPH
PSP causes early falls and axial rigidity but is characterised by vertical supranuclear gaze palsy and midbrain atrophy on MRI; tap response would not be expected in true PSP
Active malignancy mandates exclusion by CSF cytology and gadolinium-enhanced MRI; iNPH is supported when CSF cytology is negative on adequate sampling
Shuffling gait overlaps, but absence of resting tremor, asymmetric rigidity, or L-dopa response and presence of magnetic gait + DESH favour NPH

Cognitive decline overlaps; AD typically presents with episodic-memory predominance and hippocampal atrophy rather than frontal-subcortical pattern and magnetic gait; CSF biomarkers / amyloid PET resolve copathology

differential.diagnosis: Cerebral atrophy with secondary ex-vacuo ventriculomegaly
differential.key_features: Ventriculomegaly proportionate to sulcal widening, callosal angle >90°, and absence of DESH or transependymal signal argue against true NPH

optimal_actions.action: Brain MRI — measure Evans index, callosal angle, assess DESH pattern; exclude mass effect, hydrocephalus from secondary cause, and atrophy
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Ventriculomegaly with Evans index >0.3, DESH pattern (tight high-convexity sulci + widened Sylvian fissures), callosal angle <90°, periventricular transependymal signal; no mass effect or aqueductal obstruction

optimal_actions.action: Reversible-cause labs (TSH, B12, RPR, HIV) to exclude metabolic / infectious dementia mimics
optimal_actions.expected_finding: TSH, B12, RPR, HIV negative or within normal range; reversible mimics excluded

optimal_actions.action: Baseline neuropsychological battery — subcortical/frontal pattern, and reference for pre/post-tap comparison
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Frontal-subcortical pattern: executive dysfunction and slowed processing predominate over episodic amnesia

optimal_actions.action: Large-volume lumbar puncture (30-50 mL tap test) with opening pressure and pre/post gait + neuropsych assessment
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Opening pressure <25 cmH2O (normal); 30-50 mL CSF removed; pre/post tap gait and neuropsych assessment shows objective improvement supporting shunt-responsive iNPH

optimal_actions.action: Neurosurgery consultation for VP shunt candidacy and perioperative planning
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Neurosurgery accepts patient for VP shunt evaluation with programmable valve

optimal_actions.action: Amyloid PET (optional) — screen for AD copathology that may temper cognitive (but not gait) shunt benefit
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Inform shunt prognosis: AD copathology common (~50% iNPH)

useless_tools.rationale: EEG is non-specific for NPH and does not distinguish from neurodegenerative alternatives in this chronic gait/cognitive presentation
ECG is unrelated to the diagnostic workup of chronic gait + cognitive + urinary triad once cardiogenic syncope is not on the differential
Echocardiography does not contribute to NPH evaluation in the absence of syncope or cardioembolic stroke workup
Head CT is inferior to MRI for measuring Evans index and callosal angle and for excluding secondary causes; only justified if MRI is contraindicated
Cardiac monitoring has no diagnostic role in NPH and is reserved for syncope or arrhythmia workup

sequence_constraints.reason: MRI must precede large-volume LP to exclude mass effect or secondary obstructive hydrocephalus before removing 30-50 mL of CSF
Baseline neuropsychological and gait assessment must be obtained before the tap test so that pre/post change can be measured (tap response is the shunt-response predictor)

critical_actions: Obtain brain MRI before lumbar puncture to exclude mass effect or obstructive hydrocephalus
Document objective pre-tap gait (TUG and 10-metre walk) and neuropsychological baseline so that pre/post-tap change can be quantified
Remove 30-50 mL of CSF during the tap test (a low-volume LP under-samples and biases the test toward false negative)
Re-assess gait and cognition 1-4 hours after the tap and again at 24 hours (the response window for tap-test prediction of shunt benefit)
Refer to neurosurgery for VP shunt evaluation when imaging, clinical, and tap-test criteria support iNPH
contraindicated_actions: Do not perform large-volume lumbar puncture before MRI excludes mass effect or obstructive hydrocephalus
Do not infer iNPH from ventriculomegaly alone — DESH, callosal angle <90°, and a clinical triad are required
Do not diagnose Alzheimer's disease in a patient with gait-predominant presentation and ventriculomegaly without first excluding NPH
Do not attribute the syndrome to 'normal ageing' or 'deconditioning' once the imaging criteria for ventriculomegaly are met
Do not commit to iNPH without ruling out leptomeningeal disease by CSF cytology when active or recent malignancy is in the history
key_reasoning_points: iNPH diagnosis (Relkin 2005 INPH Study Group) requires (a) Hakim's triad of gait disturbance, cognitive impairment, and urinary urgency/incontinence — gait is typically first and most prominent; (b) ventriculomegaly with Evans >0.3 and DESH on MRI without mass effect; (c) age >40 and chronic course; (d) opening pressure <25 cmH2O; (e) absence of an alternative explanation
MRI is the imaging modality of choice — measure Evans index and callosal angle (<90° supports NPH) and confirm DESH (tight high-convexity sulci + wide Sylvian fissures)

The tap test is a 30-50 mL large-volume LP with pre/post objective gait (TUG, 10-metre walk) and neuropsychological assessment; opening pressure must be normal (<25 cmH2O) to satisfy the 'normal pressure' criterion
Tap-test sensitivity is only 50-80%; a single negative tap does not exclude NPH — an extended (3-5 day) lumbar drainage trial can resolve borderline cases
Reversible-cause labs (TSH, B12, RPR, HIV) are mandatory before attributing the syndrome to NPH
Approximately 50% of iNPH patients have AD copathology — this lowers cognitive benefit from shunting but does not negate gait benefit
Shunt response is best predicted by an objectively positive tap test or extended drainage trial in a patient who meets imaging and clinical criteria
